before.title: 722.9 7G-Tronic Conductor Plate (TCM) Failure and Limp Mode
before.description: The 722.9 7G-Tronic automatic transmission fitted to ML350, ML500/550 and other gasoline M-Class models uses an internal conductor plate that doubles as the transmission control module and houses the input/turbine speed sensors. Heat, ATF breakdown and vibration cause the molded-in speed sensors and the plate's electronics to degrade internally. The transmission then loses the ability to monitor input-shaft speed and torque-converter slip, producing harsh, delayed or 'thumping' shifts that start out intermittent and eventually become permanent. In the worst case the transmission locks into a single gear (typically 2nd) and enters limp mode. This is one of the most widely reported 7G-Tronic faults across the W164/W166 M-Class. Repair is plug-and-play once codes are cleared with a STAR/equivalent scanner.
before.solution: Diagnose with a Mercedes STAR (or equivalent) scanner. Replace or refurbish the conductor plate (TCM); the connecting 13-pin transmission plug/adapter and ATF + filter are usually replaced at the same time. After installation the stored transmission and body codes MUST be cleared with the scanner or the car will remain in limp mode. Rebuilt/refurbished conductor plates are a much cheaper alternative to full valve-body or transmission replacement.

before.title: Brake-Booster-Integrated Brake Light Switch Causing ESP and Cruise Control Faults
before.description: Unlike the earlier W163, the W164 M-Class no longer uses a separate, serviceable brake-light switch; the function is integrated into the brake booster assembly. When this booster-mounted switch/sensor signal degrades, owners experience a cluster of warning messages - ESP/BAS inoperative, cruise control disabled, 'run-flat indicator inoperative' - and sometimes erratic brake-light behavior or a no-start. Because the switch cannot be individually replaced, diagnosis can be confusing, and the symptom set overlaps with ABS pump and wheel-speed-sensor faults that are also common on these models. A scan tool is required to pin down the cause.
before.solution: Read fault codes with a capable scan tool to distinguish the brake-switch/booster signal fault from ABS pump or wheel-speed-sensor faults. If the booster-integrated switch is at fault, the brake booster assembly is replaced (the switch is not separately serviceable on W164). Verify and clear codes, then road-test ESP/BAS and cruise functionality.

before.title: Front Control Arm Bushing and Ball Joint Wear (Steering Wander and Clunk)
before.description: The W164 and W166 M-Class front suspension uses multiple control arms with press-fit rubber bushings and integrated ball joints (the W166 lower arm has three bushings; the upper arm has two bushings plus a ball joint). The rubber bushings dry out, crack and wear, and the ball joints develop play. Owners report clunking over bumps, knocking when turning or reversing, a 'wandering' front end and vague/loose steering as the suspension moves through excess play before the wheels respond. Given the heavy SUV weight, these wear items are commonly needed, and worn bushings/ball joints will fail an inspection.
before.solution: Lift the vehicle and check each wheel for play (top-to-bottom and side-to-side) to isolate worn bushings vs ball joints. Replace the affected upper/lower control arms (often supplied as complete arm + bushing + ball joint assemblies). Perform a four-wheel alignment afterward. Replace in axle pairs for balanced handling.

before.title: M276 V6 Timing Chain / Tensioner Rattle on Cold Start
before.description: The M276 3.5L V6 used in the W166 ML350 develops a brief but distinct rattle on cold start-up. After the car sits, oil drains from the front timing covers to the sump, leaving the secondary chain tensioners momentarily without pressure on startup. The result is chain/adjuster rattle for 1-3 seconds at first fire. Underlying contributors can include failed chain tensioners, worn camshaft adjusters, a stretched timing chain and/or worn guide rails. If ignored, severe cases risk chain/guide damage. Mercedes addressed this in TSB LI05.10-P-056435 by adding oil check valves to the tensioner oil-supply passages.
before.solution: Per the TSB, install check valves in the tensioner oil-supply openings on both cylinder heads to keep oil in the tensioners overnight; this is required regardless of which components are replaced. Inspect and, where worn, replace the chain tensioners, camshaft adjusters/solenoids, timing chain and guide rails. Use correct-spec oil and maintain oil-change intervals.
symptoms: Rattle/clatter for 1-3 seconds on cold start
Intermittent startup rattle after sitting overnight

before.title: OM642 Diesel Intake Swirl Flap and Linkage (Swirl Rod) Failure
before.description: The OM642 3.0L V6 diesel in the ML320/350 CDI and BlueTEC uses intake manifold swirl flaps actuated by plastic linkage rods ('swirl rods') and an electric swirl motor. Constant under-hood heat cycling makes the plastic linkage brittle, while carbon and oil from the crankcase breather make the flaps sticky; the combination snaps the plastic rods. Oil weeping from the turbo inlet seal can also drip onto and kill the swirl motor. The result is rough idle, power loss, an illuminated MIL and possible failed emissions inspection - a relevant concern for EU diesel periodic inspection.
before.solution: Replace the broken plastic swirl rods with upgraded metal/aluminium swirl rods (direct fit, far more durable) and clean carbon from the flaps and intake. Replace a failed swirl flap motor if oil-contaminated and address the turbo inlet seal leak that caused it. As a stop-gap some owners fit a ~4.7k-ohm resistor across the swirl-motor connector to satisfy the ECU, though this does not restore swirl-flap function.

before.title: Rear Tail Lamp Seal Water Intrusion Destroying Rear SAM and Lift-Gate Modules
before.description: On the W164 M-Class (and related X164 GL), the rear tail lamp gasket seals fail and the power lift-gate hydraulic arm boot develops stress cracks. Water then runs down inside the rear quarter and tailgate area directly onto the rear Signal Acquisition Module (SAM), the rear fuse box, the power lift-gate control module and the lift-gate hydraulic pump. Once soaked, these modules corrode and fail, producing a cascade of electrical faults. Mercedes issued a recall for MY2009 vehicles (thicker tail-lamp seal + relocated lift-gate control unit), but many earlier and unrepaired cars still suffer. Critically, replacing a water-damaged SAM without first fixing the leak will simply destroy the new module.
before.solution: Find and fix the water source first: replace the tail lamp gasket/seals with the updated thicker seal and inspect/replace the cracked tailgate lift-arm rubber boot. Dry out the area, then test and replace the rear SAM, rear fuse box, power lift-gate control module and/or hydraulic pump as needed. Clean or replace corroded connectors. Modules typically require coding after replacement.
symptoms: Power windows or lights not working

before.title: AIRMATIC Air Suspension Strut and Compressor Failure
before.description: The AIRMATIC air suspension on the M-Class is prone to air spring leaks and compressor failures, identical to issues on other Mercedes SUVs. The rubber air spring bladders crack from age and road debris, causing the vehicle to sag and the compressor to overwork. The M-Class weight accelerates wear on all suspension components.
before.solution: Replace leaking air springs and the compressor if it has failed. Consider replacing all four air springs simultaneously. Arnott and Bilstein offer quality aftermarket alternatives. Some owners convert to conventional coil springs using conversion kits to eliminate the air suspension entirely.

before.title: Transfer Case Chain Wear and Whining Noise
before.description: The 4MATIC transfer case chain in the M-Class stretches over time, producing a noticeable whining noise that increases with speed. The chain drives the torque split between front and rear axles, and excessive stretch causes imprecise torque distribution and eventually transfer case failure. Regular fluid changes help prevent premature chain wear.
before.solution: If caught early, a transfer case fluid change can slow progression. Advanced chain wear requires transfer case removal and rebuild or replacement. The chain, sprockets, and bearings should all be replaced during a rebuild. Use only Mercedes-approved transfer case fluid.
symptoms: Whining noise that increases with vehicle speed
Transfer case fluid dark or metallic

proposal.title: Transfer Case Chain Wear and Whining Noise
proposal.description: The exact M-Class transfer-case communications identify light-load vibration or jolting caused by modified oil quality in vehicles with a variable transfer case. They prescribe fault checks, an isolation drive, a fluid change and calibration when indicated. They do not establish stretched chains, speed-dependent whine, imprecise torque distribution or a universal chain, sprocket and bearing rebuild across model years 2006-2015.
proposal.solution: Record whether the complaint is vibration, jolting or whine and its load, speed and temperature. Confirm the transfer-case type, process drivetrain faults and follow the Mercedes isolation, oil-change and calibration procedure when applicable. If noise persists, diagnose bearings, gears, chain and adjacent driveline separately. Do not buy a chain, bearing kit, transfer case or fluid kit from this page; the frozen hardware identity and fitment are unresolved.
symptoms: complaint type and operating state documented
